procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated 08.09.2022 of the High Court of Delhi at New Delhi in BA No. 2675 of 2022.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The High Court of Delhi at New Delhi rejected Bail Application No. 2675/2022 on 08.09.2022.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant approached the Supreme Court after the High Court rejected their bail application. The Supreme Court granted special leave to appeal, heard the appeal with the consent of both parties' counsel, and ultimately allowed the appeal.

directions: the appellant is directed to be enlarged on bail, subject to such conditions as the trial court may impose

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court erred in rejecting the appellant's application for bail.

facts: The appellant had been incarcerated for over 7 years for offences under the NDPS Act.
The criminal trial had made little progress, with 34 more witnesses yet to be examined, despite a High Court direction to expedite it.
The appellant was not found in possession of any narcotic drug at the time of his arrest.
The main accused and another co-accused in the case had already been granted bail by the High Court.
The High Court had previously denied bail, finding a prima facie case based on call records showing contact with co-accused and bank transfers from the main accused.
law: Under Section 37 of the NDPS Act, bail can be granted only if the court is satisfied there are reasonable grounds to believe the accused is not guilty and is not likely to commit any offence while on bail.
application: The Supreme Court considered the appellant's arguments for bail, which were based on the long period of incarceration, the slow progress of the trial, and the principle of parity, as other co-accused were already on bail.
The Court weighed the prolonged pre-trial detention of over 7 years and the unlikelihood of the trial concluding soon against the strict conditions for bail under the NDPS Act.
By allowing the appeal, the Court gave significant weight to the extensive delay in the trial and the long period the appellant had already spent in custody.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court had erred in rejecting the bail application. It allowed the appeal and directed the appellant to be released on bail, primarily due to the extensive period of his incarceration (over 7 years) and the significant delay in the criminal trial.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court erred in rejecting the appellant's application for bail.
appellant_arguments: The appellant relied on precedents set in cases such as Supreme Court Legal Aid Committee v. Union of India, Shaheen Welfare Association v. Union of India, and Satender Kumar Antil v. Central Bureau of Investigation, which concern the rights of undertrial prisoners and principles of bail.
respondent_arguments: Bail should be rejected based on the gravity of the alleged offences and the severity of the potential punishment.
The appellant was in regular contact with the other co-accused to commit the crime.
Material witnesses had not yet been examined.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court concluded that statutory restrictions on bail, such as those in Section 37 of the NDPS Act or Section 43-D(5) of the UAPA, cannot indefinitely fetter a constitutional court’s power to grant bail when an accused's fundamental right to a speedy trial under Article 21 is violated. When the legislature imposes stringent bail conditions, it creates a corresponding and bounden duty on the State to ensure that such trials are concluded within a reasonable time. If the period of pre-trial detention becomes unduly long, particularly approaching half the maximum sentence, continued deprivation of personal liberty becomes a violation of the fundamental rights guaranteed by Article 21.
legal_tests_applied: A balancing test between the societal interest in restricting liberty for serious crimes and the individual's presumption of innocence and right to a speedy trial under Article 21.
The principle that statutory restrictions on bail are upheld on the condition that the trial is concluded expeditiously.

The threshold where continued pre-trial detention becomes a violation of Article 21, particularly after the accused has been imprisoned for half of the maximum possible punishment for the alleged offence.
policy_considerations: When the legislature sacrifices personal liberty for community protection through stringent bail laws, it is imperative that investigation and trials are concluded swiftly.
If the period of deprivation of personal liberty pending trial becomes unduly long, the fairness assured by Article 21 would receive a jolt.

It is the obligation of the State to proceed with cases with reasonable promptitude, particularly because a large majority of accused individuals come from poorer and weaker sections of society and may not have access to competent legal advice.
